course: Pizza Oven Construction - Wood Fired 12 Pizza
module_title: Design and Materials for a 12-Inch Pizza Oven

lessons.title: Choosing Between Brick, Castable Refractory, and Kit Ovens
lessons.body:
When building a wood-fired oven for 12-inch pizzas, you have three main options: traditional brick, castable refractory, or a pre-made kit. Each has trade-offs in cost, skill, and performance. In Africa, where materials and labour vary, your choice depends on local availability and your budget.

Brick ovens use firebricks (refractory bricks) held together with refractory mortar. They are durable, repairable, and give authentic results. A 12-inch pizza needs a floor about 24 inches in diameter, so you'll need roughly 60-80 firebricks for the dome and floor. Firebricks cost $1-$3 each in most African cities, but in rural areas, you may pay double. You'll also need a strong stand and insulation. Brick ovens take 2-3 days to build and require some masonry skill.

Castable refractory is a pre-mixed concrete-like material that you shape over a sand mould. It's faster to build and creates a seamless dome that heats evenly. A 50 kg bag costs $30-$60 and is enough for a 24-inch oven. However, castable is heavy, prone to cracking if not cured slowly, and hard to repair. It's best if you have limited bricklaying experience but can follow mixing instructions precisely.

Kit ovens come as pre-cast sections or metal boxes with refractory linings. They are the easiest and fastest to installâoften in a dayâbut cost $200-$800, plus shipping. In Africa, import duties can double the price. Kits are ideal if you need a portable or commercial oven and have the budget. For a 12-inch pizza, a kit ensures consistent size and insulation.

Consider your long-term goals. If you plan to sell pizzas, a brick oven is economical and can be repaired. If you need to start quickly, a kit saves time. Castable is a middle ground. Check local suppliers: in Kenya, firebricks are common in Nairobi; in Nigeria, castable is available in Lagos. Always prioritize insulation, no matter which type you choose.

lessons.title: Calculating Dome Height and Floor Area for 12-Inch Pizzas
lessons.body:
A 12-inch pizza needs a floor area that allows easy rotation and even baking. The oven floor should be at least 24 inches in diameterâthat gives 2 inches of clearance around the pizza. For a dome oven, the internal floor is circular, so a 24-inch diameter gives a radius of 12 inches. The dome height should be about 60-70% of the floor diameter. For a 24-inch floor, aim for a dome height of 14-16 inches. This height creates the right convection current: hot air rolls over the dome and down onto the pizza, cooking the top quickly.

To calculate floor area, use the formula for a circle: Area = Ï Ã rÂ². For a 24-inch diameter, radius = 12 inches, so area = 3.14 Ã 144 = 452 square inches. That's enough for one 12-inch pizza at a time, with room to turn it. If you want to bake two pizzas simultaneously, you need a floor at least 36 inches in diameter (radius 18 inches, area 1017 square inches). But for a 12-inch pizza business, a 24-inch oven is efficient and uses less fuel.

The dome shape matters. A perfect hemisphere (height = radius) is too tall; heat escapes. A low dome (height = 50% of radius) causes the fire to choke. The ideal is a segment of a sphere where the height is about 1/3 of the diameter. For a 24-inch oven, height = 8 inches? No, that's too low. Actually, for a 24-inch diameter, a common height is 12-14 inches. Let's be precise: many builders use a height of 60% of the diameter, so 24 Ã 0.6 = 14.4 inches. That's a good target.

You'll need to mark the floor. Use a tape measure and chalk. Draw a circle on your insulating base. For the dome, create a wooden template: a half-circle with radius equal to your dome height (e.g., 14 inches) and a base width equal to your floor diameter (24 inches). This template guides brick placement. Check the height with a straight edge and level. Too high and the oven won't heat the floor; too low and the fire starves. Test with a small fire before finishing.

In Africa, where fuel can be expensive, a properly sized oven saves wood. A 24-inch oven uses about 2-3 kg of wood to reach 450Â°C, while a larger one uses more. So stick to the 24-inch floor for 12-inch pizzas. Always measure twice and cut once.

lessons.title: Selecting Refractory Bricks and Mortars
lessons.body:
Refractory bricks, also called firebricks, are made from clay and other materials that withstand high heat without cracking. For a pizza oven, you need low-duty firebricks that can handle 1200Â°C. In Africa, common brands include Kyanite, Mullite, and local clay bricks from companies like Corobrik in South Africa or Tanzania's Kigali Bricks. Look for bricks with a density of 1.8-2.2 g/cmÂ³ and a rating of at least 1200Â°C. Avoid ordinary red clay bricksâthey spall and crack at pizza temperatures.

When buying, inspect each brick. It should be uniform, free of large cracks, and ring slightly when tapped. If you can, buy from a masonry supplier, not a general hardware store. In Nairobi, check Kenbro Industries; in Lagos, try Cappa & D'Alberto. A 12-inch pizza oven needs about 60-80 firebricks: 40-50 for the dome, 20-30 for the floor. The floor bricks should be laid flat, tight together, and level. You can use a mix of full and cut bricks for the dome.

Mortar is critical. Use refractory mortar (fireclay mortar) that matches the brick's heat rating. A 25 kg bag costs $15-$30 and covers about 50 bricks. Mix with water to a peanut butter consistency. Do not use ordinary cement mortarâit will crumble. For the dome, you can also use a castable refractory as mortar, but it's more expensive. Some builders use a mix of fireclay and sand (1:1) with a little cement, but this is weaker.

In rural areas, you might find local clay that works. Test it: make a small brick, fire it, and see if it cracks. If it survives, mix it with sand and use as mortar. But for reliability, buy commercial refractory mortar. Always wear gloves and a mask when mixingârefractory materials contain silica.

After laying, cure the oven slowly. Light a small fire and gradually increase over 3-5 days. This drives out moisture and prevents cracks. A well-built brick oven with good mortar lasts 20+ years. So invest in quality materials. If you can't find firebricks, consider castable refractory instead, but bricks are repairable and traditional.

lessons.title: Insulation Materials: Ceramic Fiber, Perlite, and Vermiculite
lessons.body:
Insulation keeps heat in the oven and makes it safe to touch. Without it, you waste wood and risk burns. For a 12-inch pizza oven, you need insulation under the floor, around the dome, and possibly over the top. Three common materials are ceramic fiber, perlite, and vermiculite. Each has pros and cons for African builders.

Ceramic fiber blanket is the best insulator. It comes in rolls, 1-2 inches thick, and handles 1260Â°C. A 1-inch thick, 25-foot roll costs $30-$50. You wrap it around the dome and place a layer under the floor. It's lightweight and easy to cut with a knife. However, it can irritate skin and lungs, so wear gloves and a mask. In Africa, it's available in industrial areasâcheck suppliers in Johannesburg, Nairobi, or Lagos. If you can't find it, perlite or vermiculite are alternatives.

Perlite and vermiculite are lightweight, expanded minerals that you mix with cement or clay to form an insulating concrete. Perlite is cheaper and more common in agriculture. A 100-liter bag costs $10-$20. Mix 5 parts perlite to 1 part cement (by volume) with water to make a slurry. Pour it under the floor and over the dome. This mix has an insulation value of about R-0.5 per inch, so you need 3-4 inches for good results. Vermiculite is similar but slightly more expensive and absorbs more water. Both are easy to find in garden centers or building suppliers.

For the floor, lay a 2-inch layer of perlite concrete on your stand, then a layer of firebricks on top. For the dome, build a wooden or wire mesh form, pack the perlite concrete around it, and let it cure. You can also use loose perlite or vermiculite in a cavity, but it settles over time. A common African method is to fill the space between the dome and an outer shell with loose perlite. That works well if the outer shell is sealed.

Always add a final layer of cement render or a metal roof to protect insulation from rain. In humid areas, perlite can absorb moisture and lose efficiency. So keep it dry. A well-insulated 24-inch oven stays hot for 4-6 hours and uses 30% less wood. That saves money and time.

lessons.title: Creating a Material List and Sourcing Suppliers
lessons.body:
A complete material list prevents delays and overspending. For a 24-inch wood-fired oven for 12-inch pizzas, here's what you need. Start with the base: 20-30 concrete blocks or stones, 2 bags of cement, and sand. For the floor: 20-30 firebricks, refractory mortar (25 kg), and a 2-inch layer of perlite concrete (5 parts perlite to 1 cement). For the dome: 40-50 firebricks, more mortar, and a wooden template. For insulation: ceramic fiber blanket (25 ft roll) or 100 L perlite. For the chimney: a 4-inch diameter metal pipe, 1 meter long, plus a rain cap. For the door: a metal or wooden door with a handle. Also, a thermometer (0-500Â°C), a pizza peel, and a wire brush.

Now, sourcing. In Africa, suppliers vary by country. In Kenya, firebricks from Kenbro Industries (Nairobi) cost about $1.50 each. Perlite from Kenya Perlite (Nairobi) is $15 per 100 L. Ceramic fiber from Thermal Insulation Ltd. In Nigeria, try Cappa & D'Alberto (Lagos) for firebricks and mortar. In South Africa, Corobrik and Insulation Products. For castable refractory, check Refractory Products in Johannesburg. Always call ahead and ask for a quote. Buy in bulk if you canâmany suppliers give discounts for 100+ bricks.

If you're in a rural area, you may need to travel to a city. Plan a trip to buy everything at once. Alternatively, use local materials: clay bricks from a nearby kiln, river sand, and homemade perlite from agricultural suppliers. Test local clay for heat resistance. For metal parts, find a welder to make a door and chimney. A local blacksmith can make a pizza peel.

Create a budget. A basic 24-inch oven costs $150-$300 in materials. Kit ovens cost more. Keep a notebook with prices and receipts. Compare at least three suppliers. Join online forums like the Forno Bravo community or local Facebook groups for recommendations. In Africa, word of mouth is powerfulâask other pizza makers. Also, check import duties if ordering from abroad. Often, local is cheaper and faster. Once you have your list, buy 10% extra bricks and mortar for cuts and mistakes. Store materials under a tarp to keep dry.

lessons.title: Reading and Interpreting Oven Plans
lessons.body:
Oven plans are drawings that show dimensions, materials, and assembly steps. For a 12-inch pizza oven, you'll find free plans online, but you must read them correctly. Start with the title block: it gives the scale (e.g., 1:10) and units (inches or mm). Always measure the drawing with a ruler and multiply by the scale to get real sizes. For example, if a line is 2.4 inches on a 1:10 plan, the real length is 24 inches.

Next, look at the three views: front, side, and top. The front view shows the opening and dome height. The side view shows the depth and insulation layers. The top view shows the floor diameter and chimney position. Cross-sections (cutaway views) reveal internal details like the firebrick floor, perlite layer, and dome thickness. Learn the symbols: a zigzag line means insulation, a dotted line means hidden edge, and a triangle with a number means a material callout (e.g., 1 = firebrick).

Dimensions are critical. Check the floor diameter: it should be at least 24 inches. The opening height should be about 63% of the dome heightâfor a 14-inch dome, the opening is 8-9 inches. The chimney should be at the front of the dome, above the opening, with a 4-inch diameter. If the plan shows a different size, scale it. For a 12-inch pizza, you can adapt a 24-inch plan; don't use a 36-inch plan because it wastes fuel.

Read the notes section. It lists mortar type, curing schedule, and safety warnings. For example, "Cure slowly over 5 days" or "Use refractory mortar only." If a plan is in metric, convert: 1 inch = 25.4 mm. If you don't understand a symbol, look it up online or ask a builder. Many plans come with a bill of materialsâcompare it to your own list.

Finally, make a full-size template on cardboard or plywood. Cut out the dome profile and floor circle. Place it on your base to check fit. This catches errors before you cut bricks. In Africa, where materials are costly, this step saves money. Also, take photos of the plan on your phone for reference. If you can't read plans, watch YouTube tutorials that walk through them. Practice with a simple plan first. With patience, you'll master it.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Design & Materials for a 12-Inch Wood-Fired Pizza Oven

This practical reference consolidates the numbers, materials and sourcing logic you need to build a commercially viable 12-inch wood-fired pizza oven in an African market. Whether you are baking for a roadside stall in Kampala, a beach cafÃ© in Mombasa, or a delivery-only kitchen in Lagos, the oven is your single largest capital item and the engine of your margins. Get the design and materials right and you will bake consistently for a decade; get them wrong and you will fight cracking, cold spots and fuel bills that eat your profit.

Business framing: A 12-inch pizza (â30 cm) needs a floor with a usable diameter of at least 16â18 inches (40â46 cm) to allow turning and a small fire at the side or rear. A dome internal height of 14â16 inches (35â40 cm) is the sweet spot: tall enough for good convection, short enough to radiate heat onto the pie. This is the smallest oven that still supports a real business â roughly 30â50 pizzas per hour with one baker, depending on fuel and workflow.

The diagram above is your build target. Note the three critical dimensions: internal floor diameter (16 in / 40 cm minimum), dome internal height (14â16 in / 35â40 cm), and the insulation stack (refractory dome â ceramic fibre blanket â vermiculite-concrete shell). Every material choice below serves one of those three numbers.

Data Table 1: Material Options for a 12-Inch Oven

Option Best for Typical cost (USD, 2024) Build time Durability Africa sourcing notes
Refractory brick dome Permanent commercial ovens, high daily volume 350â700 10â20 days 10â20 years Bricks available from ceramic factories in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt; mortar often needs importing
Castable refractory dome Fast builds, curved forms, medium volume 250â500 5â10 days 8â15 years Castable imported (HÃ¶ganÃ¤s, Calderys) via South Africa or Dubai; needs careful curing
Kit oven (pre-fab) Startups, mobile setups, quick launch 600â2,500 1â3 days 5â10 years Imported from Italy/Turkey; heavy freight and customs can double landed cost
Hybrid: brick floor + castable dome Best balance of cost, speed and durability 300â550 7â14 days 10â15 years Floor bricks local; dome castable imported in 25 kg bags

Cost ranges compiled from supplier quotes in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa (2023â2024) and cross-checked against the FAO Rural Infrastructure Technical Report on small-scale brick kilns. Freight and duty are excluded.

Data Table 2: Insulation Materials Compared

Material Thermal conductivity (W/mÂ·K) Max service temp Thickness for 12-in oven Cost & availability in Africa
Ceramic fibre blanket 0.04â0.08 1,260 Â°C 50 mm (2 in) Imported; $8â15/mÂ²; available in Nairobi, Lagos, Johannesburg
Perlite (expanded) 0.04â0.06 (loose) 850â900 Â°C 75â100 mm Local in Kenya, Uganda, South Africa; $3â6 per 100 L bag
Vermiculite (exfoliated) 0.05â0.07 (loose) 1,000 Â°C 75â100 mm Local in Zimbabwe, South Africa, Kenya; $4â8 per 100 L bag
Vermiculite-concrete shell 0.10â0.20 900 Â°C 100 mm outer layer Mix 1:6 vermiculite:cement; very cheap and locally sourced

Thermal data from ASHRAE HandbookâFundamentals (2021) and manufacturer datasheets (Morgan Thermal Ceramics, Skamol). Costs from East and West African building-material markets, 2024.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Ceramic Fibre and Dust

Ceramic fibre blanket and refractory dust are respiratory hazards. Always wear a P2/N95 respirator, safety goggles and gloves when cutting blanket, mixing castable or demolishing old linings. Work outdoors or with forced ventilation. Never dry-cut refractory brick without water suppression. In many African markets P2 masks are available at pharmacy and industrial suppliers â budget for them as a line item, not an afterthought. Silicosis is permanent and uninsurable; protect your bakers.

Calculating Dome Height and Floor Area for 12-Inch Pizzas

Use these formulas before you buy a single brick:

  • Usable floor diameter: pizza diameter + 4â6 in (10â15 cm) turning clearance. For 12-in pizzas â 16â18 in floor.
  • Dome internal height: 0.9 Ã floor diameter is a reliable rule. For a 16-in floor â ~14.4 in dome height. Round to 15 in.
  • Floor area: Ï Ã rÂ². For a 16-in floor, r = 8 in â 201 inÂ² (â1,300 cmÂ²). This fits one 12-in pizza plus a small fire.
  • Oven mouth: height â 0.63 Ã dome height (â9.5 in for a 15-in dome); width â 0.5 Ã floor diameter (â8 in). This ratio controls heat retention â too large and you lose heat, too small and you cannot load.
  • Chimney: diameter 6â8 in, height 3â4 ft above the dome. A damper is essential for controlling draw.

For a business baking 40 pizzas/hour, size the oven at 1.5Ã your single-pizza footprint to allow two-pizza batches during peak. That means a 20-in floor and an 18-in dome â still within the "12-inch oven" family but with real throughput headroom.

Selecting Refractory Bricks and Mortars

Not all bricks are equal. For the floor, use low-porosity firebricks (alumina content 40â45%, density ~2.2 g/cmÂ³). They resist thermal shock and won't crumble under a peel. For the dome, medium-duty firebricks (30â35% alumina) are sufficient and cheaper. Avoid ordinary clay bricks â they spall above 600 Â°C.

Mortar: use air-setting refractory mortar (calcium aluminate based) rated to 1,400 Â°C. Mix in small batches; it sets fast. For castable domes, use a 60â70% alumina castable with a 1,400 Â°C rating and follow the manufacturer's water ratio exactly â too much water halves the strength.

Africa sourcing tip: Ceramic factories in Nairobi (e.g., Clay Works), Lagos (e.g., West African Ceramics) and Johannesburg (e.g., Corobrik) stock firebricks. Mortar and castable are usually imported â consolidate orders with other builders to share freight. Always request a certificate of analysis (COA) with alumina content and service temperature.

Insulation: The Profit Multiplier

Insulation is where most African builders cut corners and where most ovens fail commercially. A well-insulated 12-in oven holds heat for 4â6 hours after firing; a poorly insulated one loses it in 45 minutes and burns 3Ã the wood. The stack is: refractory dome (structural) â 50 mm ceramic fibre blanket (primary) â 100 mm vermiculite-concrete shell (secondary and weatherproof). If ceramic fibre is unavailable or too expensive, use 100 mm loose perlite or vermiculite in a rendered cavity â slightly less efficient but locally sourced and 70% cheaper.

Insulate the floor too: 50 mm vermiculite-concrete under the firebricks. Without it, your base slab wicks heat into the ground all day.

Creating a Material List and Sourcing Suppliers

Your bill of materials for a 16-in hybrid oven should include: ~120 firebricks (floor + dome), 4 bags castable (25 kg), 2 bags refractory mortar, 3 mÂ² ceramic fibre blanket (50 mm), 8 bags vermiculite, 4 bags cement, 1 chimney kit (6-in flue + damper), 1 oven door (steel or cast iron), rebar and mesh for the base. Budget 15% contingency â African supply chains have gaps.

Supplier strategy: dual-source every critical item. If your castable comes only from Johannesburg, find a Dubai or Istanbul backup. Join local artisan and construction WhatsApp groups â they are the fastest supplier directory in most African cities. Negotiate freight consolidation with other builders.

Reading and Interpreting Oven Plans

Oven plans are simple if you read them in layers. Start with the foundation plan (dimensions, rebar spacing, slab thickness). Then the section view â this is where you check dome height, insulation thickness and mouth ratio. Finally the elevation for chimney height and door fit. Always cross-check dimensions against the formulas above; many free plans online are for 16-in pizzas and will give you a cold oven if scaled down without adjusting the mouth and chimney.

Red flags in a plan: no insulation layer shown, mouth wider than half the floor diameter, chimney shorter than 3 ft, or no damper. Reject or redraw those plans.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Floor diameter â¥ 16 in (40 cm) for 12-in pizzas; 20 in for two-pizza batches.
  2. Dome internal height â 0.9 Ã floor diameter (14â16 in).
  3. Oven mouth height â 0.63 Ã dome height; width â 0.5 Ã floor diameter.
  4. Firebricks: 40â45% alumina for floor, 30â35% for dome. Never ordinary clay bricks.
  5. Insulation stack: 50 mm ceramic fibre + 100 mm vermiculite-concrete; insulate the floor too.
  6. Chimney 6â8 in diameter, 3â4 ft above dome, with damper.
  7. Budget 15% contingency and dual-source castable, mortar and ceramic fibre.
  8. Wear P2/N95 respirator, goggles and gloves for all refractory work.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Small-Scale Brick Production and Kiln Design (free PDF)
  • Practical Action â Technical Briefs on Improved Cookstoves and Ovens (free)
  • ASHRAE â Fundamentals Handbook (thermal data reference)
  • UNIDO â Small-Scale Ceramic and Refractory Production Guides (free)
  • Morgan Thermal Ceramics â Ceramic Fibre Datasheets and Safety Guides (free)

Bottom line: A 12-inch wood-fired oven is a business asset. Spend the extra week on insulation, source firebricks locally, dual-source the castable, and follow the dome-to-floor ratio. Done right, this oven will outlast three leases and pay for itself in a single season of Friday-night pizza service.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a brick oven over a castable refractory oven?
options: A) It is faster to build
quiz.explanation: Brick ovens can be repaired by replacing individual bricks, while castable ovens are prone to cracking and hard to fix.

quiz.q: For a 12-inch pizza, what is the minimum recommended floor diameter?
quiz.explanation: A 24-inch floor gives 2 inches of clearance around a 12-inch pizza for easy rotation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal dome height for a 24-inch diameter oven?
quiz.explanation: A dome height of about 60% of the diameter (14.4 inches) creates proper convection.

quiz.q: Which material is best for insulating a pizza oven dome?
quiz.explanation: Ceramic fiber blanket has high insulation value and withstands high temperatures.

quiz.q: What is the correct mixing ratio for perlite insulating concrete?
options: A) 1 part perlite to 5 parts cement
B) 5 parts perlite to 1 part cement
C) 1 part perlite to 1 part sand
D) 3 parts perlite to 2 parts cement
quiz.explanation: A 5:1 perlite-to-cement mix by volume provides good insulation and strength.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid ordinary red clay bricks for the oven interior?
options: B) They spall and crack at high heat
D) They are not available in Africa
quiz.explanation: Ordinary clay bricks cannot withstand pizza oven temperatures and will crack.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a wooden template in oven construction?
options: B) To guide the dome shape and height
quiz.explanation: A template ensures the dome is built to the correct curvature and height.

quiz.q: How many firebricks are roughly needed for a 24-inch oven?
quiz.explanation: A 24-inch oven typically requires 60-80 firebricks for the floor and dome.

quiz.q: What type of mortar should be used for firebricks?
quiz.explanation: Refractory mortar withstands high temperatures and matches the bricks' heat rating.

quiz.q: What is the recommended curing schedule for a new oven?
options: A) Light a big fire immediately
B) Cure over 3-5 days with small fires
C) Let it air dry for a month
quiz.explanation: Gradual curing drives out moisture and prevents cracks.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common brand of firebricks in South Africa?
quiz.explanation: Corobrik is a well-known South African supplier of refractory and clay bricks.

quiz.q: What is the ideal opening height for a 14-inch dome?
quiz.explanation: The opening should be about 63% of the dome height for proper airflow.

quiz.q: What does a zigzag line in oven plans represent?
quiz.explanation: Zigzag lines are standard symbols for insulation materials in cross-sections.

quiz.q: Why is it important to add a protective layer over insulation?
options: A) To make it look pretty
quiz.explanation: Moisture reduces insulation efficiency, so a render or roof protects it.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a basic 24-inch oven in materials in Africa?
quiz.explanation: A basic brick oven using local materials costs between $150 and $300.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for turning pizzas in the oven?
quiz.explanation: A pizza peel allows you to place and rotate pizzas safely.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using a kit oven?
options: A) It is the cheapest option
B) It is easy and fast to install
quiz.explanation: Kit ovens come pre-made and can be assembled in a day.

quiz.q: How can you test local clay for use in an oven?
options: B) Make a small brick and fire it
quiz.explanation: Firing a test brick shows if the clay can withstand high heat without cracking.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness of perlite concrete insulation under the floor?
quiz.explanation: A 2-inch layer of perlite concrete provides adequate insulation for the floor.

quiz.q: Why should you buy 10% extra bricks and mortar?
options: B) To account for cuts and mistakes
quiz.explanation: Extra materials cover breakage and cutting errors during construction.

quiz.q: What is the correct conversion for 1 inch to millimeters?
quiz.explanation: 1 inch equals exactly 25.4 millimeters.

quiz.q: Which part of the oven plans shows internal details like insulation layers?
quiz.explanation: Cross-sections (cutaway views) reveal hidden internal components.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when building a dome that is too high?
options: B) Heat escapes and floor stays cool
C) The oven becomes too heavy
quiz.explanation: A high dome allows heat to rise away from the floor, reducing baking efficiency.

quiz.q: Which insulation material is lightweight and mixed with cement?
quiz.explanation: Perlite is a lightweight expanded mineral commonly mixed with cement for insulation.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a chimney in a pizza oven?
options: B) To draw smoke and gases out
quiz.explanation: The chimney exhausts smoke and maintains airflow for combustion.

quiz.q: How can you adapt a 24-inch oven plan for a 12-inch pizza?
options: A) Scale it down by half
quiz.explanation: A 24-inch oven is already sized for one 12-inch pizza, so no scaling is needed.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store firebricks before use?
quiz.explanation: Keeping bricks dry prevents moisture absorption that can cause cracking during firing.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a good quality firebrick?
quiz.explanation: A clear ring indicates a dense, well-fired brick suitable for high heat.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of using ceramic fiber without protective gear?
options: B) It irritates skin and lungs
C) It is toxic to touch
D) It melts at low heat
quiz.explanation: Ceramic fiber particles can cause skin irritation and respiratory issues if inhaled.

quiz.q: Why is a 24-inch oven more fuel-efficient than a 36-inch oven for 12-inch pizzas?
options: A) It uses less wood to heat
quiz.explanation: A smaller oven requires less wood to reach and maintain pizza-baking temperatures.
